rats are poor at using egocentric or directional information in a T-maze delayed alternation task, and that they are able to maintain an egocentric representation of the maze even though the animal is moved between the sample run and the test run.
rats preferentially use place information, intramazecues, and directional cues to perform delayed alternation in the absence of distal cues.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of working memory in rats and the factors that influence the use of different types of spatial memory.
the question of whether rats can solve a spatial working memory task using only egocentric information or idiothetic memory (memory for self-motion).
the question of how animals perform on spatial working memory tasks and the nature of the information they use to perform these tasks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rats use egocentric or nonmatch-to-turn strategies only when there is no other information to be used.
egocentric or nonmatch-to-turn strategies are rarely used to solve delayed alternation tasks.
egocentric and nonmatch-to-turn working memory are not used by rats in the T-maze, even under conditions that should favor their use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rats are very good at remembering places and poor at remembering turns.
rats use egocentric and/or idiothetic working memories only when they have no choice.

The main takeaway from our work is that
rats do not have egocentric or nonmatch-to-turn working memory, but rather they use place and direction cues to solve spatial working memory tasks.
